stories.title: China's Data Centers Face Little Pushback Amid AI Boom
stories.summary: An NBC News report finds that China's data center construction boom is proceeding with little local opposition, with communities largely deferring to state decisions on siting and development even as AI-driven energy demand rises.
stories.why_it_matters: The contrast with growing community resistance in the US, Europe and parts of APAC highlights a structural speed advantage for Chinese AI infrastructure buildout: fewer permitting battles and public consultations mean faster delivery of capacity. For global competitors and investors, it underscores that China's constraint on AI compute is chips and power, not social license.

stories.title: Ottogi Carrier to Supply Cooling for 48MW Korean Data Center
stories.summary: Ottogi Carrier has been selected as the cooling solution supplier for a data center being built in South Korea's greater Seoul area.
stories.content:
![Ottogi Carrier to Supply Cooling for 48MW Korean Data Center Carrier's oil-free inverter turbo chiller 19DV series supplied to hyperscale data centers. Photo courtesy of Ohsung Carrier - Seoul Economic Daily Finance News from South Korea](https://wimg.sedaily.com/news/cms/2026/08/18/news-p.v1.20260818.2f9eefa534d545f3bd0aaeb21b11039c_P1.jpg)

Ottogi Carrier has been selected as the cooling solution supplier for a data center being built in South Korea's greater Seoul area.

The company said on the 19th that it will supply cooling solutions to a 48-megawatt data center under construction in the greater Seoul area by a global data center developer and operator active in the Asia-Pacific region. Ottogi Carrier was chosen as the supplier of high-efficiency oil-free inverter turbo chillers after a technology review and a comparison of equipment operating costs.

The oil-free inverter turbo chiller supplied by the company is high-efficiency cooling equipment that uses an environmentally friendly refrigerant. It was named Product of the Year by a North American consulting engineer in 2019 and has earned an environmental EPD certification and registration as a Singapore green building product. Beyond supplying the equipment, Ottogi Carrier plans to provide maintenance services to support the data center's operation.

The data center is planned to expand in stages to a total of 500 megawatts by 2030, starting with this 48-megawatt build. Ottogi Carrier said it intends to respond actively to the additional cooling demand that will come with future expansion.

The company said the order will accelerate its push into the domestic market for cooling artificial intelligence (AI) and hyperscale data centers. It plans to expand supply of cooling solutions tailored to data center environments — including high-efficiency chillers, air cooling and liquid cooling — for large data centers being developed in the greater Seoul area and elsewhere in the country.

"This order is an achievement that reflects comprehensive recognition of Carrier's cooling technology, energy efficiency, long-term operating economics and service capabilities amid competition with global companies," an Ottogi Carrier official said. "Starting with the 48-megawatt project, we will respond actively to phased expansion demand going forward and continue to grow orders in the domestic and overseas data center cooling markets."

stories.title: Tencent Cloud plans cloud region in Malaysia
stories.summary: Tencent Cloud plans to launch a new cloud region in Malaysia, which will offer three availability zones.
stories.why_it_matters: The move extends Tencent Cloud's Southeast Asian expansion and adds Chinese cloud competition to a Malaysian market already attracting heavy hyperscaler investment, particularly in Johor and Kuala Lumpur. Regional enterprises gain another multi-AZ cloud option, while incumbent providers face pricing and localization pressure from yet another entrant.
stories.content:
Chinese cloud provider Tencent Cloud has announced its intention to launch a cloud region in Malaysia.

The company has said the region will comprise up to three availability zones, which will be located in Johor.

![Tencent Cloud](https://media.datacenterdynamics.com/media/images/20260818043127EDT_image_1.width-358.jpg) 

The region will join Tencent's existing global network of 23 cloud regions and 66 availability zones.

According to a report from The Edge Malaysia, two of the region's availability zones will launch this week.

"Malaysia remains a key market in Tencent Cloud's growth strategy across Asia," said Bluefin Jiannan Zhao, vice president of Tencent Cloud and managing director of Tencent Cloud International for Asia Pacific. "The new Cloud Region in Malaysia will serve as a critical node within our global infrastructure, enabling enterprises to scale locally, expand regionally, and accelerate their AI-driven innovation. Through this investment, we aim to deepen our support for Malaysia's digital transformation journey and contribute to the continued growth of its AI ecosystem."

"As Malaysian enterprises accelerate their digital transformation, they increasingly want to deploy AI to address real business needs and create measurable value," added Nucky Fang, general manager of Tencent Cloud International & Tencent Cloud Malaysia. "By combining local cloud infrastructure with Tencent Cloud's AI capabilities and industry expertise, we will be able to work more closely with customers and partners to develop secure, reliable, and scalable solutions tailored to their evolving needs."

In early 2026, Tencent Cloud's CEO Dowson Tong noted that the company was looking to expand its global footprint, listing the Middle East, Asia Pacific, and Europe as locations where it was seeking to add further availability zones.

Most of Tencent's presence is in Asia, but it also has regions in North America (Silicon Valley, Virginia, Toronto), Europe (Frankfurt), and South America (São Paulo).

Competitor Alibaba Cloud launched its own cloud region in Johor, Malaysia, in June of this year. The company launched a region in Kuala Lumpur in October 2017, at the time making it the first global public cloud platform to host infrastructure in the country.

stories.title: Data Center Hardware Highlights: August 2026
stories.summary: The latest in data center infrastructure – from power and minerals to networking, CPUs, and rack-scale AI systems – shows the stack shifting toward energy, interconnects, and end-to-end efficiency.
stories.content:
The latest in data center infrastructure – from power and minerals to networking, CPUs, and rack-scale AI systems – shows the stack shifting toward energy, interconnects, and end-to-end efficiency.

August 18, 2026

![Close-up of equipment in server room Close-up of equipment in server room](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt8eb3cdfc1fce5194/blt28b469851f01a923/6a84752e65b706427829a349/Close-up_of_equipment_in_server_room.png?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale)

Data Center Knowledge’s latest hardware coverage points to a system-level rethink of AI infrastructure. Beyond GPUs, the biggest stories centered on energy, mineral supply, grid interconnects, rack-scale integration, and an oncoming network supercycle, signaling an infrastructure-first phase of AI buildouts.

Here are the most-read data center hardware stories from July through mid-August:

## ‘GPUs Suck’: Former Intel CEO Slams Data Center Hardware Limitations

At the Ai4 conference, former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger argues that the current AI hardware stack, especially GPUs paired with HBM, is power-hungry and computationally inefficient. Commentary from OpenAI leadership also highlighted constraints across manufacturing, energy, and deployment that demand a system-wide redesign.

## The Critical Minerals Crisis: AI Data Centers Face Supply Chain Strain

Critical minerals, especially copper for power distribution, are emerging as a chokepoint as AI demand surges, ore grades decline, refining capacity lags, and geopolitical risks grow. While hyperscalers’ willingness to pay can secure short-term needs, it tightens the market overall. Long-term offtakes, recycling, and diversified or domestic refining are becoming essential to future-proof builds.

## Nvidia’s $500B Infrastructure Bet Raises Power Stakes

Nvidia’s financing initiative lowers the cost of deploying GPU hardware and can push more GPU spend off operators’ balance sheets. However, it does not resolve core bottlenecks: grid interconnects, transformers, turbines, and permitting. Scarcity is shifting toward energized capacity, increasing the value of power-ready sites and existing electrical infrastructure.

![pat gelsinger on stage at Ai4 conference pat gelsinger on stage at Ai4 conference](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt8eb3cdfc1fce5194/bltff2186c65f16e0a4/6a84727dbe2550d35255227f/pat_gelsinger_-_shane_snider_photo.png?width=1400&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale)

Pat Gelsinger criticized current GPU efficiency during his keynote at the Ai4 2026 conference in Las Vegas. (Photo: Shane Snider)

## TSMC Expands Arizona Campus to $265B as AI Demand Surges

TSMC is scaling up advanced chip supply in Arizona, adding multiple fabs and packaging capacity, and ramping up 2 nm (alongside 3 nm and 5 nm). The expansion targets GPUs, CPUs, networking silicon, and custom AI accelerators.

## AMD Fires Back at Nvidia with Helios AI System, Epyc CPUs

AMD introduced Helios, an integrated rack-scale AI system combining sixth-generation Epyc 9006 CPUs with new Instinct MI455X GPUs, Pensando networking, and ROCm into a single-vendor platform designed to rival Nvidia’s Vera Rubin/NVL72. AMD claims Helios delivers higher AI compute density, more memory and scale-out bandwidth, and improved tokens-per-dollar.

![AMD EPYC processor AMD EPYC processor](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt8eb3cdfc1fce5194/bltfc9ccae70335cbf4/6a84741477eb93d4f81e8220/AMD-Epyc.jpg?width=1400&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale)

AMD’s Helios is a fully integrated rack-scale AI system featuring Epyc processors. (Image: AMD)

## Enter the Network Supercycle: Preparing Data Center Networks for AI’s Next Wave

AI clusters increasingly require multi-layer fabrics (scale-up, scale-out, and scale-across), providing 10-100 times more bandwidth, ultra-low latency, and robust congestion control to keep thousands of GPUs fully utilized. As agentic AI and always-on inference expand east-west traffic, the network becomes part of the computer. Expect major upgrades in switches, optics, topology, telemetry, and resilience.

## IBM Warns AI Infrastructure Shift Impacts Software Deals, Shares Plunge

IBM’s stock declined after it warned that Q2 revenue and EPS would miss expectations, citing customers shifting spending to hardware (servers, storage, memory) to lock in constrained supply and pricing, delaying software and consulting deals. Analysts characterized the shortfall as a market-sequencing issue and flagged execution risks in converting IBM’s AI story into software-and-services wins.

## IBM Brings Z to 19-Inch Racks as AI Reshapes Data Centers

IBM is introducing rack-mount and compact single-frame versions of its z17 and LinuxONE systems, enabling enterprises to slot mainframe components into standard 19-inch racks or deploy turnkey appliances. The form-factor shift tightens the footprint and eases cooling integration alongside existing infrastructure.

## Quantum Meets the Data Center: Hybrid Systems Take Off

Quantum hardware is pivoting from qubit-count races to tightly integrated, hybrid deployments in which QPUs are co-located and low-latency-linked with GPU/CPU systems for workload-level speedups. In practice, data centers must support cryogenics, power and heat density, and vibration isolation, while maintaining modular layouts to accommodate rapidly evolving modalities.

## A Guide to Network Redundancy in Data Centers

Resilient networking remains foundational. True redundancy requires diverse ISPs and entry paths, duplicate switches and routers, and automated failover. Bonded networking can enable near-instant continuity when components fail.

## The Big Picture

The hardware stories above depict an AI ecosystem shifting from a GPU-centric lens to an infrastructure reality defined by energy, minerals, and interconnects. Financing can accelerate purchases, but energized capacity and copper availability increasingly set the pace of deployment. Meanwhile, rack-scale systems, advanced packaging, and the network supercycle are becoming decisive levers for utilization. The competitive race now spans accelerators, power, supply chains, and end-to-end system efficiency.

stories.title: GDS Lifts EBITDA Outlook as AI-Driven Bookings Hit Record
stories.summary: Chinese data center operator GDS has raised its EBITDA outlook after AI-driven customer bookings reached a record level, thebambooworks.com reports.
stories.why_it_matters: Upgraded guidance from China's largest carrier-neutral operator suggests AI demand is translating into actual contract signings rather than speculative announcements, improving sentiment toward Chinese data center assets after a prolonged valuation slump. Investors and lenders watching the sector get a concrete data point that the Chinese AI buildout is monetizing.
stories.content:
![GDS does data centers](https://thebambooworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/GDS-0818.jpg)

*China’s largest third-party data center operator reported a 838 million yuan second-quarter profit, as it doubled its 2026 sales target and raised its full-year guidance*

#### **Key Takeaways:**

- GDS Holdings posted net income of 837.6 million yuan in the second quarter, with its net margin rising to 27.1%
- The data center operator’s new bookings hit 470 MW in the first half of 2026, exceeding all of 2025, prompting management to double its full-year sales target to 1 GW

By Teri Yu

**GDS Holdings Ltd.** (GDS.US; 9698.HK), the Shanghai-based operator of high-performance data centers, sustained its growth momentum in the second quarter and raised its full-year sales target, buoyed by robust AI-related demand and contract-signing activities. The company last Thursday **reported** a net profit of 837.6 million yuan ($123.5 million) for the quarter, reversing a net loss of 70.6 million yuan a year earlier, as demand for AI computing capacity continued to reshape its business.

As China’s leading independent data center operator, GDS and its peers are at the leading edge of the AI revolution as key infrastructure providers, supporting the huge volumes of computing demand required by AI.

The company’s revenue for the three months through June rose 6.5% year-on-year to 3.09 billion yuan, while its adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) rose 2.5% to 1.41 billion yuan, translating to a healthy adjusted EBITDA margin of 45.5%. The company also recorded a 959.9 million yuan dilution gain from an external investment during the quarter.

#### **Riding the AI wave**

“We delivered solid financial and operational results in the second quarter of 2026, reflecting our continued commitment to disciplined execution,” said William Huang, GDS’ founder, chairman and CEO. “We are very excited about the opportunities in China ahead of us, driven mainly by AI demand. We are confident in our ability to capture these massive opportunities and expand our business at scale.”

The company’s core metrics all posted strong gains. Its total committed and pre-committed area rose 18.2% year-on-year to 784,802 square meters, while the utilization rate for area in service climbed to 79.2% from 77.5% a year earlier, reflecting strong sales momentum and accelerating commitment conversion. Its area under construction jumped 28.8% to 170,355 square meters, with a pre-commitment rate of 89.2%, meaning new capacity is being taken well before it comes online.

GDS’ Nasdaq-listed shares rose 6.2% to close at $34.77 on Thursday after the results came out. The stock currently trades at a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 19. Analysts expect the company’s revenue growth to accelerate to 16.4% for the year, according to the average of 24 polled by Yahoo Finance.

Strong AI demand also supercharged the company’s order book. GDS signed 260 MW of new capacity commitments in the second quarter alone, bringing first-half bookings to a record 470 MW — already surpassing the total for all last year. That momentum led management to nearly double its full-year sales target to 1 GW, up from an original goal of 500 MW.

“Our sales momentum is the strongest we have ever seen,” Huang told analysts on the company’s earnings call. He noted that GDS won significant new business from each of its three largest hyperscale customers in the first half of the year, while also beginning to build relationships with a new cohort of “emerging AI leaders.” Roughly half of its first-half bookings came from newer markets such as Ulanqab and Horinger in the Inner Mongolia region, and Shaoguan in Guangdong province, illustrating how GDS is diversifying its geographic footprint to chase demand where power and land are available.

Beyond signed contracts, customers have also locked in an additional 600 MW of reserved future capacity this year, with management expecting total 2026 reservations to exceed 1 GW — a leading indicator the company says has historically converted into bookings at a 100% rate.

CFO Dan Newman told investors that the company’s backlog swelled to 757 MW by mid-year from 450 MW at the start of 2026, representing roughly 1.6 billion yuan of “booked but not billed” adjusted EBITDA set to flow through as new data centers are delivered and ramp up.

#### **Building for tomorrow**

To keep pace with demand, GDS raised its 2026 capital expenditure guidance to around 10 billion yuan from 9 billion yuan, saying it would fund the outlay through a disciplined mix of roughly 60% project-level debt and 40% equity. The company secured 4.9 billion yuan of new debt financing and refinancing during the quarter alone, which management said reflects a highly supportive onshore lending market.

Newman noted the company has deleveraged to 4.7 times net debt to annualized adjusted EBITDA, leaving room to fund expansion while building out its onshore asset-monetization program, including a second potential asset injection into its C-REIT vehicle currently under regulatory review.

Together with its improved financial position and access to multiple funding channels, the new financing gives GDS greater flexibility to accelerate investment in China and convert its record order backlog into operating capacity.

Looking further out, management expects net move-in volumes — the pace at which built capacity is occupied and begins generating revenue — to more than double in 2027, with growth weighted toward the second half of that year, setting up what Newman described as a “significant acceleration of EBITDA growth” heading into 2028.

For the full year, GDS lifted its revenue guidance to between 12.7 billion yuan and 13 billion yuan, up from the 12.4 billion to 12.9 billion yuan it previously targeted, implying year-on-year growth of 11.1% to 13.7%. It similarly raised its adjusted EBITDA guidance to 5.9 billion yuan to 6.1 billion yuan. On a pro forma basis stripping out one-time items, first-half adjusted EBITDA already grew 12.7% year-on-year.

“With strengthened financial standing and funding capabilities to support our business expansion, we remain focused on creating sustainable, long-term value for our business partners and shareholders,” Newman said.

With bookings running at record levels, a fast-growing backlog and China’s AI infrastructure race still in its early stages, GDS management appears increasingly convinced that the company’s best growth chapter is still ahead.

stories.title: How Indonesia Emerged as a Data Center Hotspot After Singapore
stories.summary: A Tempo.co analysis examines how Indonesia emerged as a major data center investment destination following Singapore's capacity constraints, attracting hyperscalers and developers to markets including Batam and Jakarta.
stories.why_it_matters: Indonesia's rise reflects the durable spillover effect from Singapore's earlier moratorium and ongoing land and power limits, reshaping the geography of Southeast Asian digital infrastructure. Understanding this shift matters for operators and investors allocating capital in the region, as Indonesia's scale, power availability and regulation now influence where the next wave of APAC capacity lands.
stories.content:
Reporter

August 18, 2026 | 09:25 pm

![](https://statik.tempo.co/data/2025/05/15/id_1398781/1398781_720.jpg)

**TEMPO.CO, Jakarta** - Jones Lang LaSalle (JLL) Indonesia stated that data center projects are now the second-largest contributor to industrial land demand. "Aside from manufacturing, the primary contributors are clearly those related to copper and mining, but the second-largest source of demand comes from 'other services'—specifically data centers," said Farazia Basarah, Country Head and Head of Logistics & Industrial at JLL Indonesia, during a media briefing in Jakarta on Tuesday, August 18, 2026.

Farazia recounted that, about seven years ago, the data center project was initially centered in Singapore. However, the Singaporean government imposed a moratorium on the construction of new data centers due to their substantial electricity consumption.

Ultimately, Farazia noted that investors were turning to Johor Bahru, Malaysia, and Batam, Riau Islands, to build data centers. However, rather than locating these facilities within industrial zones, investors expanded into commercial and residential areas. This sparked protests from residents, who found the developments disruptive. In response to these complaints, Farazia stated that the Johor Bahru local government has prohibited the expansive development of data centers.

As a result of this situation, Farazia stated that Indonesia is finally able to absorb demand for data centers in both Batam and Jakarta. At the same time, she noted that the government is seizing investment opportunities driven by high internet penetration and a young generation raised in the technology era—factors that are fueling the growing need for data centers in Indonesia.

Beyond its role as a data center hub, Faraiza stated that the Indonesian government does not want the country to merely serve as a provider of rental services and electricity. Instead, the government is actively encouraging the development of a domestic technology industry ecosystem. She cited the facilities at the Nongsa Digital Park Special Economic Zone in Batam as an example, noting plans to transform them into an "AI factory."

According to Farazia, the development of AI technology production centers, such as microchip production centers, is expected to generate multiplier effects, including job creation. These effects can be directly felt by the public. This is because data center projects tend to generate fewer jobs than manufacturing projects. "We do not want to end up like Malaysia—where complaints have arisen, similar to those possibly seen in the United States, regarding data center construction—due to the perception that the multiplier effect is not as significant as that of building a factory," Farazia stated.

Farazia stated that the increased demand for land for data center projects is primarily driven by the need to accommodate the surging requirements of AI. He noted that about two to three years ago, the land requirement for a single data center was only around 5 hectares; now, that demand has jumped to 10–30 hectares per facility.

Fariza estimates that the power capacity of currently built and operational data centers stands at 450 megawatts (MW). These data centers have an occupancy rate of approximately 70 percent in Jakarta's business districts and 80 percent in Cikarang, Karawang, and East Jakarta. Alongside the expansion of these facilities, Fariza notes that electricity demand for data centers is rising, reaching 100–200 megawatts per project.

To accommodate those needs, Farazia stated that PT PLN requires a lead time of approximately two years. "And that is just for a single data center," she said.

Based on the discussions, Farazia concluded that PLN has an ample electricity supply. However, the challenge lies in the procurement process for preparing infrastructure, such as transformers for substations.

stories.title: For High-Density AI, Available Data Center Space May Not Be Usable
stories.summary: North American vacancy remains at 1%, but JLL says only a very small share of that capacity can support high-density AI deployments.
stories.content:
North American vacancy remains at 1%, but JLL says only a very small share of that capacity can support high-density AI deployments.

![blue-tinted data center racks blue-tinted data center racks](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt8eb3cdfc1fce5194/bltdd0b3cf41f5a0549/6a831cb17ec7f30cef7f1f67/GettyImages-2289124609.jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale)

A 5 MW data center buyer recently approached more than 10 North American operators seeking capacity for 140-160 kilowatts per compute rack. Nearly every operator had space. Almost none could support the required density with direct liquid cooling, according to James Mercer, principal of Metro Colo Advisory, who conducted the search for a client.

Mercer agreed to be quoted on the record but declined to identify the operators, citing ongoing channel relationships with them.

The search highlights a distinction between available data center capacity and capacity capable of supporting the highest-density AI systems.

JLL’s local brokerage teams track available capacity by rack density, according to Andrew Batson, who leads the firm’s data center research. Only a “very small percent” of the 1% vacancy can support high-density deployments such as the requirement Mercer was shopping for, Batson told Data Center Knowledge. He said JLL views liquid-cooling infrastructure as a requirement for AI deployments at these densities.

## 1% Vacancy, Little AI-Ready Capacity

JLL’s Midyear 2026 North America Data Center Report puts North American vacancy at 1% for the third consecutive year. Available capacity is limited to small, fragmented blocks, while most tenants securing space are contracting for 2028 deliveries. More than 66 GW of capacity is under construction across North America, JLL said, with 77% of that capacity in frontier markets.

For an AI buyer seeking 140-160 kW per rack, however, the market is much narrower than the headline vacancy rate suggests.

“Most vacancies are in legacy products,” Batson said. Over a multiyear horizon, JLL expects more AI-enabled capacity to come online. The gap between nominal vacancy and AI-ready capacity is unchanged, he noted.

## Few Facilities Can Support 100 kW+ Racks

Uptime Institute’s 2025 Global Data Center Survey found that 82% of respondents had a highest-density rack below 30 kW, while only 9% reported a highest-density rack of 50 kW or more. Uptime identified some cabinets exceeding 100 kW but said those remained rare.

“Probably a low single digit (under 4%) of data centers in the US can currently support these racks,” said Daniel Bizo, research director at Uptime Intelligence, Uptime Institute’s market research unit. Bizo told Data Center Knowledge that the figure is an inference from Uptime’s survey data and should be treated as indicative due to sample size limitations. Uptime’s surveys show fewer than 1% of operators running 100 kW+ racks as a standard configuration, Bizo said. Fewer than one in 10 US operators may be able to support a limited number of 100 kW racks, such as a single row.

“With AI computing for training still proliferating, 100 kW+ racks are becoming more common,” Bizo said.

That puts Mercer’s 140-160 kW requirement at the extreme end of the market.

The 30-kW threshold reflects both the statistical distribution of rack densities and changes in hardware and rack configurations needed to support denser deployments, Bizo said. Most data centers designed over roughly the past decade were built around an average rack power of about 20 kW, even if that capacity was not fully fitted on day one. Those facilities can often accommodate 30-40-kW racks in limited numbers with relatively straightforward upgrades, he said.

The picture changes above 50 kW.

“Above 50 kW, it becomes increasingly impractical to cool with air due to space limitations in the IT chassis/rack, mandating direct liquid cooling,” Bizo said.

At scale, higher-density racks also create power-distribution challenges involving larger and heavier busways and PDUs, power cables, breakers, and potentially additional circuits, he said. Electrical room size and layout can become constraints. Some components have 6- to 12-month lead times due to high demand, while additional power-distribution equipment adds weight to already heavy racks. That can create structural issues in multistory buildings.

“100 kW+ racks pose a bigger electrical challenge than thermal,” Bizo said.

Bizo added that a 140-160 kW requirement does not mean every rack in a larger deployment will operate continuously at that level. A deployment built around racks at that peak density could average about 80 kW per 19-inch rack position, since network, storage, and other racks are part of the installation. Compute racks also may not operate at maximum power simultaneously, although training workloads can produce recurring peaks that electrical systems must be sized to accommodate.

Uptime does not have a direct cross-tab that compares liquid-cooling capability with ultra-high-density rack support. Bizo said support for liquid cooling is broader than support for 100 kW+ racks, meaning liquid-cooling capability alone is not a reliable proxy for extreme rack-density capability.

More than half of US operators surveyed by Uptime brought some high-density capacity online during the 12 months through April 2026, Bizo noted. That share rises to about two-thirds for the current 12-month period. However, Uptime did not define high density specifically as racks of 100 kW+, so the figures do not directly measure the expansion of ultra-high-density capacity.

## Megawatts Aren’t Enough

A buyer seeking 5 MW at 140-160 kW per rack is not looking for generic vacant capacity. The deployment requires electrical infrastructure capable of delivering the required power at the rack, cooling systems capable of removing the resulting heat, direct liquid-cooling capability and suitable contiguous space.

Mercer’s published analysis says rack-scale GPU systems at these densities use direct-to-chip liquid cooling, with cold plates cooling processors and a coolant loop reaching the white space through a coolant distribution unit. His analysis also distinguishes between a provider saying it supports liquid cooling and a specific data hall having a liquid-cooling loop serving the white space today. That distinction matters for a buyer trying to deploy immediately.

Mercer’s search found operators with space that could not meet the required density and cooling configuration. His analysis identifies Nvidia’s GB300 NVL72 platform as requiring roughly 140-160 kW per rack. JLL’s 1% vacancy rate captures overall market availability, while Uptime’s data show how uncommon extreme rack densities remain. Neither measures the amount of vacant capacity capable of supporting a 140-160 kW rack.

## Credit Screens Further Narrow Options

The physical constraint was not the only obstacle Mercer encountered.

The two purpose-built, liquid-cooled operators he approached were the only ones in his search that engaged substantively rather than declining outright. Both asked, without prompting, whether his client was investment grade. Mercer declined to identify those operators, citing his ongoing relationships with them.

One confirmed it had no capacity for the requested timeline, mentioned a future project that might fit, and then asked whether the client was investment grade. Further discussion was contingent on the answer, Mercer said. Mercer has seen that screening on this requirement only. He does not claim it is a broader industry practice.

The observation follows an April 2026 report by Data Center Knowledge on stalled neocloud deals, which found that operators were scrutinizing customers for credit quality, long-term viability, and balance-sheet durability. The reporting found that operators were requiring stronger guarantees, including letters of credit or parent backing, and were declining some neocloud deals despite aggressive commercial terms.

The new observation raises a narrower question: When high-density capacity is already scarce, does customer credit become another filter on facilities capable of serving those deployments?

JLL’s financing analysis concerns project lending, not operators’ customer-selection policies. It does not establish that colocation providers broadly require investment-grade customers.

But tenant credit can affect how developers structure AI and high-density projects, according to Carl Beardsley, senior managing director and data centers leader at JLL Capital Markets.

Asked whether tenant credit affects how developers approach AI and neocloud customers, particularly for specialized high-density deployments, Beardsley said: “The simple answer is, yes, it does.”

“It is important for the developers to bring in an advisor or lender early in the process as they are structuring the lease to ensure it is financeable,” Beardsley said.

JLL’s latest report provides context for the financing side of that question. Construction lending remains liquid across credit tiers, including AI companies and neoclouds, JLL said. But non-credit-tenant deals are evaluated on a case-by-case basis, with debt metrics depending on the tenant profile, credit support from the off-taker, and project location. JLL said credit spreads on those deals generally run 200 to 300 basis points wider than investment-grade construction loans, with leverage of 70% to 80% of loan cost compared with as much as 85% for top-tier credit hyperscalers.

## Two Screens for Scarce Capacity

For AI developers, that leaves two potentially separate screens for scarce high-density capacity: whether a facility can physically support the workload and whether the customer can satisfy the operator’s credit requirements. Mercer’s search provides one example of those constraints appearing in the same procurement process.

stories.title: Equinix signs solar PPA with Flo Energy in Singapore
stories.summary: Equinix has signed a renewable energy power purchase agreement with Flo Energy Singapore, one of the city-state's largest independent electricity retailers, to power its Singapore facilities with solar energy. It is Equinix's fourth such agreement in Singapore in the past two years.
stories.why_it_matters: The deal shows how operators are working within Singapore's limited domestic renewable generation by contracting through retailer-aggregated PPAs, a model other constrained APAC markets may follow. Repeated PPA signings also help Equinix meet corporate sustainability targets and customer requirements for green-powered colocation in a market where renewable options are scarce.
stories.content:
Colocation giant Equinix has signed a virtual Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) with renewable energy firm Flo Energy in Singapore.

The deal will see Flo supply Equinix with at least 11.5MW of renewable energy generated from industrial and commercial rooftop solar installations across the country. The agreement also includes an option to expand the capacity to up to 50MW.

![Equinix Flo Energy](https://media.datacenterdynamics.com/media/images/1787037161802.width-358.jpg) 

"Singapore’s position as a trusted global AI and digital hub will be underpinned by digital infrastructure that is resilient, sustainable and built for the future," said Yee May Leong, managing director, Singapore, Equinix. "Our fourth PPA is a significant milestone that reflects the power of collaboration across Singapore's public and private sectors. As demand for digital infrastructure continues to accelerate, Equinix remains committed to supporting Singapore's position as a global digital hub while advancing the nation's sustainability goals."

The PPA was Flo’s first under its newly launched Data Centre Solutions offering, which is also available to data center operators in Australia through Flo's local business.

Following the latest PPA, Equinix now has a contracted capacity of 215MW across Singapore, all of which is expected to come online in 2028. Collectively, these agreements are expected to generate about 250,000MWh of electricity per year. It has previously signed PPAs with Sembcorp (x2) and TEPCO.

The company has also engaged in national renewable initiatives, including SolarNova 7 and JTC Jurong Island.

Equinix currently operates five data centers in Singapore (SG1, SG2, SG3, SG4, and SG5). It has a sixth facility, dubbed SG6, currently under development, and is slated for completion in Q1 2027.

stories.title: Data Centers Account for 80% of Industrial Land Demand in Indonesia
stories.summary: Data Centers Account for 80% of Industrial Land Demand Tempo.co English
stories.content:
Reporter

August 18, 2026 | 05:50 pm

![](https://statik.tempo.co/data/2023/06/23/id_1214200/1214200_720.jpg)

**TEMPO.CO, Jakarta** – Data center projects accounted for 80 percent of demand for industrial land in Indonesia over the past year, driven by the rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI), according to property consultancy Jones Lang LaSalle (JLL) Indonesia.

“Data center demand has increased over the past year due to the growth of AI,” JLL Indonesia Country Head and Head of Logistics & Industrial Farazia Basarah said at a media briefing in Jakarta on Tuesday, August 18, 2026.

Farazia highlighted a significant surge in land requirements for data center projects. She said the amount of land needed had increased from around five hectares two to three years ago to between 10 and 30 hectares per data center today.

Data centers currently have a combined operational capacity of around 450 megawatts (MW), with occupancy rates of about 70 percent in Jakarta’s central business districts (CBDs) and 80 percent in Cikarang, Karawang and East Jakarta, she said.

As data center footprints expand, their electricity requirements have also grown, reaching 100 to 200 MW per project. Farazia said state electricity company PT PLN (Persero) requires a lead time of around two years to meet the electricity needs of a data center.

“And that is only for one data center,” she said.

According to discussions with industry players, Farazia said PLN still had sufficient electricity supply. The main challenge, she said, was the procurement process required to prepare supporting infrastructure, including transformers for substations.

### AI fuels data center expansion

Farazia said the rapid expansion of data centers was closely linked to growing demand for AI infrastructure. The pace of development has been so fast that changes are becoming visible not only year to year but also from one quarter to the next, she said.

Despite the surge in data center demand, JLL recorded continued positive demand across Indonesia’s industrial and logistics sectors, with occupancy reaching 95 percent.

In the second quarter of 2026, JLL recorded 7.55 hectares of newly supplied industrial land, while demand stood at around 3.56 hectares.

“Besides manufacturing, the main contributors are clearly sectors related to copper and mining. But the second-largest source of demand comes from other services, particularly data centers,” Farazia said.

She said demand for industrial and logistics space remained resilient in the second quarter, supported by foreign direct investment (FDI), which accounted for 50 percent of investment in the manufacturing sector.

Manufacturing FDI also grew 7 percent year on year in the second quarter, further supporting demand for industrial and logistics facilities, she said.

stories.title: Groq raises $350m, with Nvidia participation "planned"
stories.summary: Company value nearly halved following Nvidia license deal
stories.content:
AI inference company Groq has raised $350 million, at a $3.5 billion valuation.

The company develops its own SRAM-heavy inference chips, which it offers from 13 data centers across North America, Europe, the Middle East, and Asia Pacific. The round was led by Disruptive, with "planned participation" from Nvidia.

![Jensen Huang's signed Nvidia Groq 3](https://media.datacenterdynamics.com/media/images/Jensen_Huang_Groq_3.width-358.png) 

The fundraising comes despite Nvidia licensing all of the company's technology on Christmas Eve last year, in a $20bn deal that also saw the GPU giant hire founder and then-CEO Jonathan Ross, along with president Sunny Madra and other members of the Groq team.

Nvidia plans to launch its own Groq-based hardware later this year, and then develop more advanced chips based on Groq, but with an expanded team and utilizing Nvidia IP, including NV Link.

The departure of its leadership and the creation of a major rival has impacted Groq's valuation. In September before the deal, Groq raised $650m in a round again led by Disruptive, but at a $6.9bn valuation.

“We are building Groq into the world’s leading AI inference cloud," Alex Davis, Disruptive CEO and Groq executive chairman, said after this week's round.

"We look forward to continuing our partnership with Nvidia at such an important juncture for the ecosystem. Inference will without a doubt become the largest and most critical layer of AI infrastructure. Our team has unmatched experience operating LPUs at scale and delivering the performance, efficiency, and reliability that the next generation of AI demands. We will be focused on supporting the most important model makers to further contribute to the global growth of innovation and American ingenuity.”

Groq remains an Nvidia Cloud Partner (NCP), certified to design, deploy, and operate Nvidia accelerated computing to Nvidia’s reference architecture and operational standards.

The company said that it hopes to scale from 54MW of compute to 200MW+ in 2027.

stories.title: Nvidia Backs OpenAI Data Center With $105 Billion, Denies Circular Financing
stories.summary: Nvidia is backing OpenAI's data center buildout with up to US$105 billion in investment, according to the Seoul Economic Daily, and has denied that the arrangement constitutes circular financing.
stories.why_it_matters: The deal tightens the financial interdependence between the AI sector's dominant chip supplier and its largest model developer, a structure critics argue inflates demand signals across the AI infrastructure market. For APAC data center operators and investors, it reinforces that OpenAI-linked capacity demand will continue to flow into the region, while raising questions about how durable that demand is if AI spending expectations reset.
stories.content:
![Nvidia Backs OpenAI Data Center With $105 Billion, Denies Circular Financing Nvidia and OpenAI logos. Reuters/Yonhap News - Seoul Economic Daily International News from South Korea](https://wimg.sedaily.com/news/cms/2026/08/18/rcv.YNA.20260817.PRU20260817273701009_P1.jpg)

[[B1]] SILICON VALLEY — Nvidia has cut the guarantee it will provide for OpenAI's long-term leased data center to $105 billion, about half of earlier estimates, but concerns persist. Chief Executive Jensen Huang pushed back, calling it an effort to secure infrastructure to support long-term demand, yet investors remain uneasy.

[[B2]] OpenAI, the developer of ChatGPT, said on the 17th that it had signed a deal with SB Energy and Nvidia to secure 8 gigawatts of infrastructure at the "Potts Pike" data center campus in Pike County, Ohio. Under the arrangement, SB Energy builds the data center and OpenAI leases it for 20 years. Of the 8GW, 800 megawatts of computing capacity will begin operating around 2028.

[[B3]] The Potts Pike data center is a flagship project led by the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump and SoftBank, the parent company of SB Energy, and will be built out to 10GW, the largest in the world. One gigawatt is equivalent to a single nuclear reactor, enough to power 750,000 to 1 million households.

[[B4]] The part of the deal drawing the most attention is the "residual value guaranties" agreement between Nvidia and SB Energy. Nvidia will guarantee up to $105 billion (about 149 trillion won) of the value of the data center that SB Energy is building. Nvidia will provide credit support to SB Energy in return for exclusively supplying its AI chips, and the guarantee will shrink as OpenAI pays its rent. If OpenAI withdraws or fails to pay rent, SB Energy will find a new tenant or resell the facility, with Nvidia bearing 25% of any losses that remain. Early in the deal, projections had put the potential guarantee at up to $250 billion, so the figure has been sharply reduced.

[[B5]] The $105 billion applies to the initial 4.25GW phase of the project, and additional support could follow for the remaining 3.75GW. Nvidia stressed that "a 4.25GW AI factory could correspond to about 1.5 million Nvidia GPUs, or $150 billion to $200 billion in Nvidia revenue," and said that combined with chips already agreed to be purchased, it could generate about $600 billion in revenue for Nvidia through 2030. Separately from the guarantee, Nvidia will also invest $1.5 billion in SB Energy.

[[B6]] Whenever Nvidia has invested in private AI developers such as OpenAI and Anthropic, or in cloud companies such as Nebius, controversy over circular financing has flared. The structure had companies borrowing Nvidia's money, using Nvidia's chips, and channeling the resulting revenue back to Nvidia.

[[B7]] Apparently mindful of the controversy, Huang rebutted the circular-financing criticism in a blog post. Asked whether it was circular financing, Huang said it was not and that OpenAI would pay the rent. Huang added that the arrangement uses economies of scale and long-term demand forecasts to secure Nvidia's computing resources, and that Nvidia commits core resources when it can accurately predict customer demand and lock in long-term production capacity.

[[B8]] Some observers argue the circular-financing debate could resurface because, even without directly funding the deal, Nvidia is spurring chip sales. Following Nvidia's announcement, the stock closed flat that day.

[[B9]] Jeffrey Gundlach, chief executive of DoubleLine Capital and known as the "new bond king," wrote on his X account, formerly Twitter, on the 15th that assets with uncertain lifespans, referring to AI chips, cannot serve as collateral for long-term debt. He added a jab, comparing the use of AI chips as collateral to issuing 30-year asset-backed securities against a warehouse of bananas.

stories.title: Tasmania Launches Parliamentary Inquiry into AI Data Centres
stories.summary: Tasmania's House of Assembly Standing Committee on Government Administration A has opened a formal parliamentary inquiry into the construction and operation of AI data centres, with submissions being accepted from 5 August. The inquiry comes as Firmus Technologies advances plans for multiple large-scale AI facilities in the state.
stories.why_it_matters: The inquiry puts one of Australia's most aggressive AI data center buildouts under political scrutiny, creating regulatory uncertainty for Firmus and other developers banking on Tasmania's cool climate and renewable energy. The outcome could set precedents for how Australian states weigh energy use, environmental impact and economic benefit in approving large AI facilities.
stories.content:
Tasmania’s Parliament has launched a formal inquiry into the construction and operation of AI data centres, opening the sector to parliamentary scrutiny as AI infrastructure company Firmus Technologies progresses plans for multiple large-scale facilities across the state.

The **House of Assembly’s Standing Committee on Government Administration A commenced the inquiry** on 5 August, with submissions opening on 18 August and due by 21 September. The committee has been tasked with examining the construction and operation of AI data centres and recommending any legislation or regulation needed to protect public resources and the environment, improve planning arrangements, increase parliamentary oversight and transparency, provide opportunities for community consultation and ensure Tasmania receives tangible benefits from the facilities.

The inquiry is not specifically directed at Firmus, but its establishment comes as the company advances a three-site expansion in northern Tasmania that is expected to become a significant new electricity load for the state. The committee is chaired by Labor MP Brian Mitchell, with Greens MP Tabatha Badger as deputy chair. Other members are Labor MP Anita Dow, Liberal MPs Michael Ferguson and Mark Shelton, and independent MPs Helen Burnet and Professor George Razay.

### Greens had pushed for inquiry

The Greens have been campaigning for a parliamentary inquiry for several months, linking their concerns directly to Firmus’s plans and the broader expansion of AI infrastructure in Tasmania. In June, Greens MP Tabatha Badger announced the party’s intention to seek an inquiry, citing concerns over energy and water consumption, community consultation and the absence of specific regulation governing AI data facilities.

The Greens subsequently tabled a motion seeking greater transparency around the Tasmanian government’s commitments to Firmus, while also pushing for information about the company’s energy and water requirements. The motion passed the House of Assembly unanimously in May.

### Firmus expansion brings scrutiny

Firmus is currently constructing its Project Southgate AI factory at St Leonards near Launceston and has proposed additional facilities at Bell Bay and Wesley Vale. The company describes the Tasmanian development as a multi-stage AI infrastructure programme. Its Bell Bay plans involve two purpose-built AI data hall buildings on the former Gunns pulp mill site, while the Wesley Vale proposal is for an AI factory on part of the former Wesley Vale Pulp Mill industrial site.

The scale of the proposed electricity demand is central to the parliamentary debate. During Budget Estimates in June, energy minister Nick Duigan said Firmus’s three planned stages were expected to require “in the realm of 400 megawatts” of electricity, noting that Aurora Energy already had a 104MW contract with the company.

The first St Leonards facility is already under construction. Firmus has said its initial northern Tasmanian stage is being delivered in two steps reaching a combined 90MW, with a further 300MW stage planned subject to approvals.

Firmus’s plans have already prompted questions in political circles over how the additional electricity demand will be supplied. In June, Duigan told Tasmania’s Legislative Council that the government’s expectation was that substantial new electricity loads would bring new generation with them, and said Firmus understood the need to bring forward generation to support its planned load. The Federal government’s March AI infrastructure expectations similarly call on new data centres to secure additional clean energy generation and/or storage to offset their demand.

The issue has also extended to water. Firmus’s proposed use of Tasmanian irrigation water for its AI facilities was questioned publicly in July, after Tasmanian Irrigation said it had given the company no undertaking to supply water and that its existing scheme was intended for agricultural use and hydrogen production. Firmus has subsequently published its own energy and water policies and says its facilities are designed around renewable energy and high-efficiency cooling.

### Inquiry scope

The committee’s terms of reference go beyond individual projects and could ultimately influence how Tasmania regulates the sector more broadly. Among the matters being examined are whether the state’s Resource Management and Planning System adequately recognises the specific impacts of AI data centres, how resource consumption should be disclosed publicly, how Parliament should oversee future facility construction and resource allocation, and what benefits should flow to Tasmanian communities.

The committee can also recommend future legislation and regulations. That makes the inquiry significant for Tasmania’s emerging data centre market, where the state has historically promoted its renewable electricity resources as a competitive advantage. The Tasmanian government’s investment agency continues to market the state on its access to renewable energy, industrial land and a stable operating environment.

Tasmania had already established a dedicated policy approach to data centres before the latest parliamentary inquiry. Industry research platform Certified Strategic recently identified Tasmania, alongside Victoria and South Australia, as one of three Australian jurisdictions with a dedicated data centre policy instrument, with Tasmania’s approach centred on its AI Factory Zone in the north.

The inquiry could now test whether that investment-focused approach provides sufficient safeguards as the scale of proposed AI infrastructure increases. For Firmus, the parliamentary scrutiny comes just as its Tasmanian rollout is moving beyond its original Launceston project. The company is developing Bell Bay and Wesley Vale as additional sites, while also investing in connectivity: Firmus and SUBCO announced in June that they would build the Bernacchi-1 submarine cable, connecting Tasmania into SUBCO’s mainland SMAP network.

stories.title: APAC Data Center Pipeline Hits Record 26.5 GW Amid AI Surge
stories.summary: The Asia-Pacific data center development pipeline has reached a record 26.5 GW, driven by surging demand for AI computing capacity across the region.
stories.why_it_matters: A pipeline of this scale confirms APAC as the fastest-growing data center theater globally and raises the stakes on power availability, land and grid connection timelines across the region's key markets. Developers, utilities and regulators now face pressure to deliver capacity on schedule or risk pushing hyperscale investment toward markets that can.
stories.content:
### Tightening Supply and Pre-Leasing Trends

Despite the delivery of about 1.4 GW of new operational capacity during the period, colocation vacancy rates in the region declined from 10.9% in the second half of 2025 to 10.3%. This indicates that customer demand is quickly absorbing new supply, with a growing share of capacity being pre-leased before facilities become operational.Pritesh Swamy, head of research and consulting at Cushman & Wakefield's Asia-Pacific data center group, noted that new supply is being absorbed rapidly. He added that power constraints, extended development timelines, and evolving technical requirements are prompting customers to commit to capacity well in advance of project completion.

### Regional Construction and Market Dynamics

Southeast Asia accounts for roughly half of all capacity under construction in APAC, with 2.38 GW. Malaysia leads the region with 1.04 GW under construction, followed by Thailand with 859 MW. Johor, Indonesia, and Bangkok are key hubs for this expansion.Johor's capacity under construction increased by 91% to 602 MW, with its overall development pipeline growing 28% to 3.09 GW. When combined, existing and future capacity in Johor surpasses 4 GW, positioning it as the largest market in Cushman's APAC maturity index.Mumbai's data center pipeline expanded 31% to 1.73 GW, reflecting significant growth in India's key market. Japan added 293 MW of operational capacity, reaching a total of 1.8 GW and surpassing India to become APAC's second-largest operational market after mainland China.Cushman & Wakefield projects that Australia, India, Japan, and Malaysia will each exceed 2 GW of operating capacity by 2028. Greater Seoul recorded a particularly tight colocation vacancy rate of just 1.1% in the first half of 2026, with its pipeline remaining nearly flat despite a 10% rise in operational capacity.

### Power Constraints and Shifting Development

The report highlights that the composition of the pipeline is critical, with approximately 82% still in the planning phase rather than under construction. The delivery of this planned capacity is heavily dependent on factors such as power connections, land availability, permitting, financing, and equipment supply, indicating that APAC has entered a period of "power-constrained execution."While data centers historically clustered around network connectivity, the demands of AI infrastructure require significantly greater electrical capacity and higher-density cooling. This is prompting a shift in development from saturated hubs towards peripheral districts and new markets capable of providing power at scale. Despite these shifts, established hubs like Tokyo (4.4% vacancy) and Singapore (4.8% vacancy) continue to experience strong demand, though land and power constraints are limiting conventional expansion. Swamy reiterated that power and land constraints are increasingly influencing where new capacity can be built, encouraging developers and hyperscalers to explore secondary markets offering scalable resources.

stories.title: DayOne Secures US$415 Million Green Loan from DBS, OCBC and UOB for Hydrogen-Powered Data Center in Singapore
stories.summary: DayOne has secured a SGD 530 million (US$415 million) green loan from DBS, OCBC and UOB to fund a proof-of-concept hydrogen-powered data center in Singapore, its first facility in the country. The project will integrate on-site Solid Oxide Fuel Cell technology for hydrogen-based power generation.
stories.why_it_matters: The deal marks the first time Singapore's three major banks have jointly financed hydrogen-based generation for a data center, setting a template for how alternative power technologies can be funded in a market where grid capacity and land are severely constrained. If the proof of concept succeeds, it could reopen Singapore to new data center development that bypasses traditional grid limitations.
stories.content:
Singapore-based data center platform DayOne has secured SGD 530 million (US$ 415 million) green loan from Singapore-based leading banks DBS, OCBC and UOB to support a first-of-its-kind proof of concept for hydrogen-based power generation in a data center in Singapore. The data center, DayOne’s first in Singapore will integrate Solid Oxide Fuel Cell (SOFC) technology on-site.

DBS, OCBC and UOB are acting as Joint Mandated Lead Arrangers and Bookrunners, as well as Green Loan Coordinators for the four-year green loan. DBS is also serving as the Facility and Security Agent, according to the banks’ press release.

Located in the western part of Singapore, the 20-megawatt (MW) data center, SG1, broke ground in July 2025 and is expected to be ready for service by Q1 2027. It will feature vertical building-integrated photovoltaics (BIPV) and incorporate hybrid air and liquid cooling technologies to increase energy efficiency.

In December 2025, the facility was awarded BCA Green Mark Platinum (Provisional) certification, the highest Green Mark rating awarded by Singapore’s Building and Construction Authority under the Green Mark for Data Centres Scheme.

DayOne’s footprint spans across Asia and Europe, covering Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, Japan, Hong Kong, Finland and Spain.

![](https://w.media/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Issue-13-Banner-1-1024x201.jpg)

Han Kwee Juan, Group Head of Institutional Banking, DBS, said: “Demand for digital infrastructure is accelerating as AI and cloud computing continue to reshape economies across Asia. Drawing on our expertise in financing digital and renewable infrastructure projects, we are pleased to partner DayOne and the bank consortium to finance Singapore’s first data centre to pioneer a proof-of-concept for hydrogen-based energy. Singapore is well-positioned to lead financing of green and energy efficient digital infrastructure in Asia.”

Elaine Lam, Head of Global Corporate Banking, OCBC, said: “Singapore’s first data centre incorporating hydrogen power represents an important milestone in the evolution of sustainable digital infrastructure. As demand for digital services and connectivity continues to grow, innovative energy solutions will play an increasingly important role in supporting this growth sustainably. This financing reflects OCBC’s commitment to supporting technology sectors, including digital infrastructure, which are increasingly critical to economic development, while advancing energy transition solutions that enable sustainable growth.”

Edmund Leong, Head of Group Corporate Banking and Sector Solutions Group, UOB, said: “This financing supports next-generation infrastructure that will strengthen Singapore’s position as a leading AI and digital hub while advancing sustainability goals.”

stories.title: Panduit Confident of Meeting Data Center Infrastructure Demand in Malaysia
stories.summary: Panduit’s new infrastructure solutions are backed by its robust local manufacturing presence, with its manufacturing facility in Johor Bahru, serving as a vital supply chain hub regionally.
stories.content:
*Panduit’s new infrastructure solutions are backed by its robust local manufacturing presence, with its manufacturing facility in Johor Bahru, serving as a vital supply chain hub regionally.*

          ![](./media_1901a7ae5285e7a8c75d7f29dded8d7bbc36b73bf.jpg?width=750&format=jpg&optimize=medium) 

As Malaysia continues to see a boom in data centers being built in the country, ensuring there is sufficient supply of components needed to power and run these data centers is imperative. While water and energy remain core components, there is also the need to have sufficient supply of the back-end hardware that supports the data centers.

This includes the network cables, racks, switches, and other key components which Panduit is seeing an increased demand in the country. Panduit’s end-to-end solutions support a wide range of critical industries in the country, including hyperscale data centre operators, several leading technology companies, and top financial institutions,

At the recent Panduit Technology Day Malaysia, the company introduced three new infrastructure solutions designed to help organizations address increasing power, connectivity, and scalability demands. They include the EL2P Intelligent Power Distribution Unit, Gen 7 SAN Director Connectivity, and Fault Managed Power System (FMPS).

Panduit also showcased its AI infrastructure readiness with the introduction of its next-generation Very Small Form Factor (VSSF) fiber optic portfolio. Featuring MMC connectivity and shuffle cables, this new range is specifically engineered to support advanced AI GPU architectures, including NVIDIA Vera Rubin. By providing higher fibre density and performance optimized for AI environments, the VSSF portfolio helps support the scalability requirements of next-generation computing environments.

According to Simin Sirun, Business Director for ASEAN, India, and Korea at Panduit, the American company working with data center developers and contractors that are building the data centers for the tenants. He said the tenants include both local and international players such as the hyperscalers.

Sirun also pointed out that Panduit is also among the top players to provide compliant and compatible products to ensure the GPU performance, including NVIDIA GPUs, is guaranteed in terms of its transmission.

“In terms of our ecosystems, we actually sell through our authorized distributor. And through the distributor, we have got our partner ecosystems in Malaysia that perform the installation. In our partner program itself, we have got platinum, gold, silver, and registered partners. We have got about 45 companies in Malaysia who support our businesses regularly on all these infrastructure build-ups, ranging from enterprise data center manufacturing facilities,” Sirun said.

## Ensuring supply chain

Given the supply chain challenges in the data center industry, especially when it comes to getting sufficient chips for GPUs and such, Sirun explained that Panduit has a strong plan in place in how it manages its supply chain.

“We have our own warehouse. We don't rely heavily on third parties, so we have our own. In Asia, for example, we have warehouses in China, in Japan, in Singapore, and in Australia too. So, for us, we have undertaken a lot of large, massive projects and we are able to do it because we have the supply chain capability and also we plan to build that,” Surin said.

He added that Panduit was also able to fulfil most customer expectations as they build the products in advance and inventoried them in their own warehouse, which is then inventoried by Panduit’s distributor partners.

“Our distributor in Malaysia is keeping a pretty high inventory right now because of the surge in demand. We want to make sure that those customers that we have committed to are able to deliver. We are engaged right at the customer, so we know exactly the timing. So, we want to make sure that the product comes before the whole execution,” he added.

Surin also mentioned that Panduit engages customers from the start to implementation.

“When you want to implement all these in data centers, it's also not easy because it's massive. You have good product; you also need to have people that know how to install properly,” he said.

Panduit’s new infrastructure solutions are backed by its robust local manufacturing presence. The company's manufacturing facility in Johor Bahru, which commenced operations in October 2023, serves as a vital supply chain hub regionally. The facility, equipped with advanced robotics, automation, and energy-efficient design practices, directly supports the objectives of Malaysia's New Industrial Master Plan 2030 (NIMP 2030) to accelerate high-value industrial growth and sustainable manufacturing.

Beyond manufacturing excellence, the Johor Bahru manufacturing facility has created over 200 employment opportunities across various sectors such as engineering, technical, and production roles, contributing significantly to the development of Malaysia’s skilled industrial workforce.

stories.title: Alibaba Cloud launches third data center in South Korea
stories.summary: Alibaba Cloud has launched its third data center in South Korea, extending a footprint it began building in the country in 2022. The expansion forms part of Alibaba Group's US$53 billion commitment to AI and cloud infrastructure investment.
stories.why_it_matters: The launch deepens Alibaba Cloud's competitive position against AWS, Microsoft and Google in a strategically important Northeast Asian market, and signals that China's largest cloud provider is pushing ahead with overseas AI infrastructure buildout despite geopolitical headwinds. Korean enterprises and AI workloads gain another hyperscale option, while local colocation and connectivity providers face intensified competition.
stories.content:
The latest addition to its South Korean cloud region comes a little more than a year after adding a second data center location.

![Alibaba Cloud Yongjoon Yoon](https://media.datacenterdynamics.com/media/images/O1CN01LUdIkAlAnKJ3eae8_6000000004255-0-tps-180.width-358.png) 

Where in the country the data centers are located has not been shared, though most of South Korea's data centers are located in and around the capital city, Seoul.

As part of the company's $53bn commitment to its global cloud footprint, the data center will significantly expand Alibaba's capacity in South Korea.

Alibaba Cloud has had a presence in the country since 2016, originally offering cloud and digital transformation services to enterprises and then launching its first data center in 2022.

The region will offer an array of cloud services, including compute, storage, networking, security, and databases, as well as AI offerings.

“South Korea is a key market where Alibaba Cloud has continued to make long-term investments,” said Yongjoon Yoon, country manager of South Korea, Alibaba Cloud Intelligence. “The third data center is not merely an infrastructure expansion. It is an investment to help South Korean enterprises operate AI and cloud-based services more reliably. Alibaba Cloud will continue to support the digital transformation of South Korean businesses with robust, scalable, and secure cloud infrastructure and AI services.”

Outside of South Korea, recent new locations Alibaba has added include France, Japan, Malaysia, and Mexico. The company now has 104 availability zones across 30 regions.

stories.title: Goodman Signs 20-Year Lease with Global Hyperscaler in Greater Tokyo
stories.summary: Goodman Group has signed a 20-year lease with an unnamed global hyperscaler for the first 50 MW phase of Tsukuba Tech Central, its planned 1 GW data center campus in Greater Tokyo. Power for the project has been secured from TEPCO.
stories.why_it_matters: A two-decade commitment at a 1 GW campus validates Greater Tokyo's emergence as a primary Japanese hyperscale market beyond central Tokyo, and gives Goodman a long-term anchor tenant to underwrite the campus's remaining phases. It also demonstrates that large power allocations from TEPCO are still obtainable, a key gating factor for Japan's data center growth.
stories.content:
Goodman Group, a global provider of digital infrastructure, has signed a 20-year lease with a global hyperscale customer for the first 50 MW phase of Tsukuba Tech Central, its 1 GW data center campus in Greater Tokyo. While the identity of the customer has not been revealed yet, power has been secured from TEPCO and diverse dark fibre routes to Greater Tokyo’s main interconnection points for Goodman’s exclusive use.

Goodman acquired the 45-hectare site in 2022 and will develop, own, fit out and operate the facility, which is under construction. It will be ready for service in early 2028. In a press release, Goodman further revealed that campus employs an efficient cooling design that uses industrial water so will not draw on Tsukuba’s groundwater. Moreover, the plant sits within acoustically enclosed structures to minimize noise.

![](https://w.media/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Japan-CDC-2026-Banner.jpg)

Paul McGarry, Head of Asia, Goodman, said, “Securing this global hyperscale customer unlocks Tsukuba Tech Central as a premier data center hub in Tokyo. We are already in advanced discussions with customers over the next phases at the campus”.

Mindful of growing concerns about power use by data centers, power for this project will be drawn from grid electricity on new power infrastructure with no impact to other users and standby generators are for rare emergency use only. Moreover, Goodman says it is continuing to work with its customers and local utilities on renewable electricity supply for the campus.

This is significant because, as AI workloads shift from training to inference, demand is concentrating in metropolitan markets close to users. Cloud demand also continues to grow, making locations such as Tsukuba Tech Central, adjacent to major population centers, highly sought after. The binding constraint in those markets is grid connection capacity where data centers are required, which takes years to secure.

![](https://w.media/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Issue-13-Banner-1.jpg)

Goodman has developed and managed property in Japan for more than 20 years, including more than 300 MW of data center projects at Goodman Business Park in Inzai, In May 2026, it was appointed lead development partner for a proposed data center campus in Sagamihara City. Japan forms a key part of Goodman’s data center platform in Asia which includes Hong Kong where Goodman has ~400 MW under management on completion of projects currently under construction.

stories.title: DayOne partners with Cortical Labs and NUS Medicine to deploy Singapore's first biological data center prototype
stories.summary: DayOne has partnered with Cortical Labs and NUS Medicine to deploy Singapore's first biological data center prototype, consisting of a 20-unit CL1 biological computing system.
stories.why_it_matters: The deployment positions Singapore as an early testbed for biological computing, a nascent field that promises dramatically lower energy consumption than conventional silicon-based processing. While still experimental, involvement from an established operator like DayOne gives the technology commercial credibility and hints at how future data centers might handle certain workloads.
stories.content:
DayOne has deployed Singapore’s first biological data center prototype, in partnership with Cortical Labs and the Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine at the National University of Singapore (NUS Medicine).

It comes five months after DayOne announced it was working with Australian biological computing startup Cortical Labs to establish two data centers in Melbourne, Australia, and Singapore.

![DayOne Cortical Labs](https://media.datacenterdynamics.com/media/images/DayOne_Cortical_Labs.width-358.jpg) 

The deployment consists of a 20-unit CL1 biological computing system, housed in a live research environment at NUS Medicine hosted by DayOne.

Launched in March 2025, the company’s CL1 system combines neurons cultivated from human stem cells with silicon to create what the company says is a “more advanced and sustainable form of AI,” a neural network dubbed Synthetic Biological Intelligence (SBI). Once cultivated, the neurons grow across the silicon chip, which sends and receives electrical impulses into the neural structure, before being integrated into Cortical Labs’ Biological Intelligence Operating System (biOS), which is capable of running simulations.

The operating system is able to send information directly to the neurons about their environment, and as they react, their impulses affect their simulated world. The neurons can then be kept alive for up to six months with the CL1’s internal life support system.

The CL1 is an upgraded version of a biological computer previously demonstrated by Cortical Labs, then known as DishBrain. That version contained 800,000 human and mouse neurons on a CMOS chip and taught itself to play Pong.

"Our commitment to Singapore goes beyond capacity. We are here to help shape what the next generation of digital infrastructure looks like, and that means investing in approaches that meet Singapore's sustainability ambitions alongside its AI ambitions. This prototype is a step toward demonstrating that scaling compute and reducing resource intensity are goals we can pursue together," said Jamie Khoo, CEO of DayOne.

Hon Weng Chong, founder and CEO of Cortical Labs, added: "The establishment of this prototype shifts the conversation from research to commercial application. Biological computing supplements AI in areas where data is sparse, learning from far less and adapting as conditions change."

Cortical Labs was founded in Melbourne in 2019 and, to date, has secured $11 million in funding, with investors including Horizons Ventures, Blackbird Ventures, LifeX Ventures, Radar Ventures, and the CIA's In-Q-Tel.

Singaporean data center operator DayOne currently runs a portfolio of more than 500MW of data center capacity in service and under construction, and more than 500MW held for future development across sites in Hong Kong, Singapore, Malaysia (Johor), Indonesia (Batam), and Japan (Tokyo). The company recently broke ground on a site in Thailand and another in Singapore. In August, it made its first foray into markets beyond Asia, announcing a campus in Lahti, Finland.

Formerly known as GDS International, DayOne rebranded as an independent company last year. The company is reportedly looking to go public in the near future. In June 2026, the company secured $4.5 billion in Series C equity financing.
